questions.question: Which organelle, described by a student using an electron microscope, was seen (A centriole, B Golgi, C rough ER, D smooth ER)?
questions.answer: B: Golgi apparatus
steps: The description "several curved membrane-bound sacs of decreasing size" matches the flattened cisternae of the Golgi apparatus, which modifies and packages proteins in pancreatic cells.
A centriole is a ring of microtubules with no membrane, so A is wrong.

Rough ER is a network of flattened sacs studded with ribosomes, and smooth ER is a tubular network with no ribosomes; neither is described as a stack of curved sacs of decreasing size, so C and D are wrong.

questions.question: Explain why this organelle cannot be seen using a light microscope.
questions.answer: The organelle is smaller than the resolution limit (about 200 nm) of a light microscope, which uses visible light.
steps: Light microscopes have a resolution limit of about 200 nm.
Organelles such as the ER are smaller than this limit.
Two points closer than the resolution appear as one.
An electron microscope uses electrons with a much shorter wavelength, giving higher resolution.

questions.question: Give two differences between an organ and a tissue.
questions.answer: An organ contains several different tissue types working together for a function; a tissue is a group of similar cells with one function.
steps: A tissue is a group of similar specialised cells.
An organ is made of several different tissues.
An organ performs a more complex function than a single tissue.
Organs are larger structures within an organism.

questions.question: Name two structures present in animal cells that are not present in plant cells.
questions.answer: Centrioles and lysosomes (cilia and flagella are also acceptable).
steps: Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.
Animal cells lack those structures.
Centrioles are found in animal cells only.
Lysosomes are also found only in animal cells.

questions.question: Explain the results of the fluorescence investigation in pancreas cells.
questions.answer: The green-labelled amino acids were taken up and built into proteins, which were then secreted: fluorescence fell inside from 100% to 38% and rose outside from 0% to 62% in 60 min.
steps: At 0 min all the marker (100%) is inside because the labelled amino acids have just been taken up by the pancreas cells.
The labelled amino acids are used to make polypeptides on ribosomes (rough ER), so the green label becomes part of the proteins.
The proteins pass in vesicles to the Golgi (modified, e.g. glycoproteins), then in secretory vesicles to the cell surface membrane and leave by exocytosis.
After 60 min fluorescence outside has risen by 62% and inside fallen by 62%, so labelled enzymes and glycoproteins have been secreted from the cells.
38% is still inside because some protein is still being made or moved through the ER and Golgi, or is retained for use in the cell.

questions.question: In which stage of meiosis does independent assortment occur (A metaphase I, B metaphase II, C telophase I, D telophase II)?
questions.answer: A - metaphase I
steps: Independent assortment is the random alignment of homologous pairs.
This happens at the equator in metaphase I.
Each pair orients either way round, independent of other pairs.
Option A is correct.

questions.question: In which stage of meiosis does crossing over occur (A metaphase I, B metaphase II, C prophase I, D prophase II)?
questions.answer: C - prophase I
steps: Crossing over happens when homologous chromosomes pair up.
Pairing and crossing over occur in prophase I.
Chiasmata form where the non-sister chromatids swap segments.
Option C is correct.

questions.question: Explain why the percentages of gametes with each allele combination are not 25% each.
questions.answer: Genes A and B are on the same chromosome, so their alleles tend to be inherited together; only crossing over produces the other combinations, in smaller proportions.
steps: Genes on the same chromosome are linked, not independently assorted.
Alleles that start on the same chromosome stay together unless crossing over occurs.
Parental combinations are therefore more common than 25%.
Recombinant combinations arise only from crossing over and are less common.

questions.question: Describe how more than one type of protein can be synthesised from the RNA produced from one gene.
questions.answer: Alternative splicing: different combinations of exons are kept when introns are removed, producing different mRNAs and so different polypeptides.
steps: Transcription produces pre-mRNA containing introns and exons.
Introns are removed by splicing.
Different exons can be included or excluded during splicing.
Each different combination gives a different mRNA.
Each mRNA is translated into a different polypeptide.

questions.question: Comment on the changes in the activity of genes T and U as a mouse zygote develops into a blastocyst.
questions.answer: Gene T falls to near zero by the blastocyst stage, while gene U stays steady then rises sharply from the morula to the blastocyst.
steps: Gene T: activity is high and fairly constant (a slight rise) from zygote to about the 4-cell stage, then falls from the 8-cell stage, dropping steeply through the morula to a very low level at the blastocyst.
Gene U: activity stays low and almost constant from zygote to the 8-cell stage, then increases slowly at the morula and rapidly at the blastocyst, to well above its early level.
So the genes are switched on and off at different stages: T is turned down as development proceeds and U is turned up.
This is differential gene expression, which allows cells to differentiate into different cell types (e.g. trophoblast and inner cell mass).

questions.question: State what is meant by the term polygenic inheritance.
questions.answer: Inheritance of a characteristic controlled by two or more genes, each with alleles that have additive effects, producing continuous variation.
steps: Polygenic means many genes.
Each gene contributes a small additive effect.
The combined effect gives a range of phenotypes.
This produces continuous variation.

questions.question: Which graph represents the distribution of mass of these beans?
questions.answer: B: a bell-shaped (normal) distribution histogram
steps: Bean mass shows continuous variation, because it is polygenic and also affected by the environment.
Continuous variation gives a normal distribution: most beans have a mean mass and few are very light or very heavy, so graph B (symmetrical, peak in the middle).
A is a steady decrease and D is a growth (sigmoid) curve; neither is a frequency distribution of mass.
C has two peaks at the extremes, which would show discontinuous (two-group) variation, not polygenic inheritance.

questions.question: Height is another example of polygenic inheritance. Adult height can be predicted in three steps: (1) add the mother's height (cm) to the father's height (cm); (2) add 13 cm if the child is a boy, or subtract 13 cm if the child is a girl; (3) divide by two. A woman who is 1.59 m tall has a daughter, and the father is 1.76 m tall. Calculate the predicted adult height of their daughter, in metres.
steps: Add the parents' heights: 159 cm + 176 cm = 335 cm.
For a girl, subtract 13 cm: 335 - 13 = 322 cm.
Divide by 2: 322 / 2 = 161 cm.

questions.question: Explain why their daughter may not grow to this predicted height.
questions.answer: Height is polygenic and influenced by many other genes, and environmental factors such as diet, health and illness also affect growth.
steps: The prediction uses only the parents' heights.
Height is controlled by many genes, not just the parents' alleles.
Environmental factors such as nutrition, disease and exercise affect growth.
So the actual adult height may differ from the prediction.

questions.question: Which labelled structure in the beta cell electron micrograph produces ribosomes (A P, B Q, C R, D S)?
questions.answer: C: R (the nucleolus)
steps: Ribosomes are made (ribosomal RNA is transcribed and assembled with proteins) in the nucleolus.
R points to the dense dark region inside the nucleus, which is the nucleolus.
Q is the stacked rough ER, P is cytoplasm with ER, and S is the nuclear envelope or chromatin region; none of these makes ribosomes.

questions.question: Suggest why the structures labelled T and U look different in the photograph, although they are the same type of organelle.
questions.answer: They are mitochondria cut in different planes: one in longitudinal section and the other in cross section.
steps: T and U are both mitochondria, which are three-dimensional sausage-shaped organelles.
The electron microscope image is a thin 2D slice, so the appearance depends on the angle of the cut.
A section cut along the length (U) looks long with cristae visible, while one cut across (T) looks circular or oval.

questions.question: Calculate the magnification of the image, given structure U measures 52 mm and is 3.0 (units garbled) long.
steps: Magnification = image size / actual size.
Convert to the same units: 52 mm = 52 000 um.
Magnification = 52 000 / 3.0 = 17 333, so about x17 000 (x1.7 x 10^4).

questions.question: Describe how insulin is transported from the ribosomes and then secreted by a beta cell.
questions.answer: Insulin is made on ribosomes on the rough ER, carried in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus, modified and packaged into secretory vesicles, which fuse with the cell surface membrane to release it by exocytosis.
steps: Ribosomes on the rough ER synthesise the insulin polypeptide.
The polypeptide enters the rough ER lumen and is folded and modified.
Transport vesicles carry it to the Golgi apparatus.
The Golgi modifies and packages insulin into secretory vesicles.
The vesicles move to the cell surface membrane, fuse with it and release insulin by exocytosis.

questions.question: Explain why beta cells can produce insulin but other cells in the pancreas do not.
questions.answer: Beta cells express the insulin gene because of differential gene expression; other pancreas cells switch that gene off and express other genes.
steps: All cells in the pancreas contain the same genome.
Cell differentiation switches on only certain genes in each cell type.
Beta cells switch on the insulin gene by transcription factors and epigenetic control.
Other cells keep the insulin gene switched off and make other proteins instead.
So only beta cells transcribe and translate the insulin gene.

questions.question: How many of the three statements about the pair of chromosomes are correct (A none, B one, C two, D three)?
questions.answer: C - two
steps: Statement 1: there are three gene loci on the pair. This is correct.
Statement 2: the pair separates into different cells after mitosis. This is wrong; in mitosis sister chromatids separate, homologous pairs do not.
Statement 3: one chromosome from each parent. This is correct.
Two statements are correct, so option C.

questions.question: Describe what happens to these chromosomes when they enter interphase.
questions.answer: The chromosomes uncoil into chromatin and each DNA molecule is replicated, forming sister chromatids.
steps: Chromosomes decondense during interphase into chromatin.
In the S phase, each DNA molecule is replicated.
Each chromosome now consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
This prepares the cell for division.

questions.question: Name the stage of meiosis in which crossing over begins.
questions.answer: Prophase I
steps: Homologous chromosomes pair up in prophase I.
Pairs form bivalents and non-sister chromatids overlap.
Crossing over (chiasmata formation) begins here.
So the stage is prophase I.

questions.question: How many of the listed allele combinations (AbE, ABe, abE, abe) could result from one crossover of the chromosomes shown?
questions.answer: B: two (AbE and abe)
steps: The chromosomes carry A b e and a b E, so there is no B allele anywhere and ABe is impossible.
A crossover between A and b or between b and e swaps the end sections of two chromatids, making the new combinations AbE and abe.
abE is just the unchanged parental chromosome, so it is not a result of crossing over; two combinations (AbE and abe) are produced.

questions.question: Explain why alleles b and e are more likely to be inherited together than alleles A and e.
questions.answer: Genes b and e are closer together on the chromosome, so crossing over between them is less likely; they stay linked.
steps: Crossing over happens between homologous chromosomes at random points.
The closer two genes are on a chromosome, the less likely a crossover between them.
b and e are closer together than A and e.
So b and e are less often separated and are inherited together more often.

questions.question: Explain how an egg cell is specialised for its function.
questions.answer: The egg is large and contains a food store (yolk) and organelles needed to support early development.
steps: An egg cell must provide food for the developing embryo.
It is large and contains a lot of cytoplasm and yolk.
It contains stored nutrients and organelles for early development.
Its haploid nucleus combines with a sperm nucleus to form a zygote.

questions.question: Compare and contrast metaphase in mitosis and meiosis.
questions.answer: Both have chromosomes lined up at the equator attached to spindle fibres; in mitosis single chromosomes align, but in meiosis I homologous pairs align.
steps: In both, spindle fibres attach to centromeres at the cell equator.
In mitosis metaphase, single chromosomes line up in one row.
In meiosis I metaphase, homologous pairs line up as bivalents.
Meiosis II metaphase lines up single chromosomes, like mitosis, but the cell is haploid.

questions.question: Explain how the cells of the beluga morula change as they develop into the cells of the blastocyst.
questions.answer: Morula cells divide and become differentiated, forming an outer trophoblast layer and an inner cell mass, with a fluid-filled cavity (blastocoel) forming.
steps: The morula is a solid ball of cells formed by mitosis.
Cells divide further and begin to differentiate.
Outer cells form the trophoblast, which later forms placental tissues.
Fluid enters the centre, forming a blastocoel; inner cells form the inner cell mass.

questions.question: Calculate the value of the term shown, using the table of chicken ages and egg masses.
steps: Fill in the missing rows: age 39 has rank 2 and mass rank 1, so D = 1 and D^2 = 1.
Age 60 has rank 9 and mass rank 2, so D = 7 and D^2 = 49.

questions.question: Calculate the correlation coefficient rs for the data using the formula.
steps: Use rs = 1 - 6 x (sum D^2) / (n(n^2 - 1)) with n = 9 pairs and sum D^2 = 159.5.
rs = 1 - 957/720 = 1 - 1.329 = -0.329, i.e. about -0.33 (a weak negative correlation).

questions.question: Explain whether the null hypothesis should be accepted or rejected, given rs = 0.38 and the critical values table.
questions.answer: Accept the null hypothesis: 0.38 is below the critical value (0.683 for 9 pairs), so there is no significant correlation.
steps: Compare the calculated rs (0.38) with the critical value for the number of pairs (0.683 for 9 pairs; 0.738 for 8 and 0.648 for 10).
If the calculated value is greater than the critical value the null hypothesis is rejected; here 0.38 is smaller than every value in the table.
So the correlation is not significant at the 95% level; any link between chicken age and egg mass could be due to chance, and the null hypothesis is accepted.

questions.question: Animals of this nematode species are either male (one sex chromosome) or hermaphrodite (two sex chromosomes). A hermaphrodite makes both sperm and egg cells: about 300 sperm are produced first and stored, then egg cells are produced. Its sperm can fertilise its own egg cells (self-fertilisation). When a hermaphrodite mates with a male, the male's sperm fertilise the egg cells, which results in 700 more fertilised egg cells than self-fertilisation; half of these fertilised egg cells give male offspring. Explain how the reproductive behaviour of these nematodes increases their chance of survival.
questions.answer: Hermaphrodites can self-fertilise, ensuring reproduction without a mate, and mating with males gives many more offspring and genetic variation.
steps: Hermaphrodites store around 300 sperm and then produce egg cells.
Self-fertilisation lets a single nematode reproduce when no male is present, ensuring survival.
Mating with a male adds about 700 more fertilised eggs, so many more offspring.
Males are produced from half of these eggs, so the population keeps both sexes.
Outcrossing mixes alleles from two parents, increasing genetic variation.
Variation improves the chance some offspring survive changing conditions.

questions.question: Deduce how histone modification can be passed onto embryos, using the two experiments shown.
questions.answer: It is passed on through the maternal chromosomes in the egg, and enzyme M in the zygote is needed to keep the modification as cells divide.
steps: In both experiments the sperm has no histone modification and the maternal chromosomes in the egg do, so the modification is passed to the embryo through the egg (maternal chromosomes), not the sperm.
Experiment 1: enzyme M is present in the egg and zygote, and after several cell divisions all maternal chromosomes still have the modification.
Experiment 2: enzyme M is absent from the egg and zygote, and the modification is reduced at every division until no chromosomes are modified.
So enzyme M must be present in the zygote and later cells to copy or maintain the modification on newly replicated histones; without it the modification is diluted at each cell division and lost.

questions.question: Calculate the volume of a spherical liposome of diameter 75 nm, in standard form.
steps: Radius = diameter / 2 = 37.5 nm.
Volume of a sphere = 4/3 x pi x r^3 (the formula is not shown in the text; standard sphere formula used).
In standard form: 2.2 x 10^5 nm3.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structures of pre-mRNA and active mRNA.
questions.answer: Both are single-stranded RNA; pre-mRNA contains introns and exons and no cap or tail, while active mRNA has introns removed, a 5' cap and a poly-A tail.
steps: Both are single-stranded polynucleotides made of ribonucleotides.
Pre-mRNA contains both introns and exons; active mRNA has only exons.
Active mRNA has a 5' cap and poly-A tail added, which pre-mRNA lacks.
Active mRNA is shorter because the introns are removed.

questions.question: State the types of division at step A and step B in the production of sperm cells.
questions.answer: Step A: mitosis; step B: meiosis
steps: The unspecialised diploid cell first divides by mitosis to make more diploid cells.
Some of these then undergo meiosis to produce haploid cells.
So step A is mitosis.
Step B is meiosis, producing haploid spermatids.

questions.question: Which part of the sperm cell contains enzymes released to break down the zona pellucida (A W, B X, C Y, D Z)?
questions.answer: A: W (the acrosome)
steps: The acrosome is a vesicle at the tip of the sperm head that contains digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes, released by exocytosis to digest the zona pellucida around the egg.
W labels the cap at the front of the head, the acrosome.
X is the nucleus (DNA), Y is the mid-piece full of mitochondria, and Z is the tail (flagellum), so B, C and D are wrong.

questions.question: Explain what happens at step D for the cell to become a specialised sperm cell.
questions.answer: Step D is differentiation: cytoplasm is lost, the nucleus condenses, the acrosome forms from the Golgi, mitochondria gather in the midpiece and a flagellum forms.
steps: The spermatid loses most of its cytoplasm, making it streamlined.
The nucleus condenses and becomes compact.
The Golgi forms the acrosome, which contains enzymes.
Mitochondria gather in the midpiece to provide ATP for the flagellum.
A flagellum (tail) forms from a centriole for movement.

questions.question: Draw a diagram to show the arrangement of cells in a blastocyst.
questions.answer: A hollow ball of cells: an outer layer (trophoblast) surrounds a fluid-filled cavity, with a clump of inner cells (inner cell mass) on one side.
steps: Draw a hollow sphere of cells.
Label the outer layer as the trophoblast.
Show the fluid-filled cavity (blastocoel) in the middle.
Show the inner cell mass as a clump on one side.

questions.question: The blastocyst contains some pluripotent stem cells. Which of the following describes these pluripotent stem cells? A adult stem cells that can give rise to most types of cell in the body, including totipotent cells; B adult stem cells that can give rise to most types of cell in the body, excluding totipotent cells; C embryonic stem cells that can give rise to most types of cell in the body, including totipotent cells; D embryonic stem cells that can give rise to most types of cell in the body, excluding totipotent cells.
questions.answer: D - embryonic stem cells that can give rise to most cell types, excluding totipotent cells
steps: Cells in a blastocyst are embryonic stem cells.
Pluripotent cells can give rise to most cell types but not to a whole organism.
Totipotent cells (e.g. the zygote) can form all cell types including extraembryonic tissues.
So option D is correct.

questions.question: Suggest why the use of stem cells from salamander embryos was approved by the ethics committee.
questions.answer: Salamander embryos are not human, so the ethical concerns about human embryos do not apply, and the cells are pluripotent so can be useful for regeneration research.
steps: Ethics committees weigh the moral status of embryos.
Salamander embryos are not human, so human-embryo concerns do not apply.
Embryonic cells are pluripotent, able to become many cell types.
This makes them useful for studying regeneration.

questions.topic: Cell Cycle Role In New Cells
questions.question: Describe the role of the cell cycle in producing new cells.
questions.answer: The cell cycle makes new genetically identical cells: interphase replicates DNA and organelles, mitosis divides the nucleus and cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.
steps: Interphase: the cell grows and replicates its DNA.
Mitosis: the replicated chromosomes are separated into two nuclei.
Cytokinesis: the cytoplasm divides into two cells.
The two daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent.

questions.question: Explain why increased methylation of the RB gene could cause the growth of a tumour.
questions.answer: Methylation silences the RB gene, so less RB protein is made; without this inhibition, cells divide uncontrollably and form a tumour.
steps: RB is a tumour suppressor gene; its protein inhibits cell division.
Increased methylation of the gene reduces its transcription.
Less RB protein is made.
Cells then divide without control, forming a tumour.

questions.question: Explain how preventing the shortening of spindle fibres affects mitosis.
questions.answer: Chromatids cannot be pulled apart to the poles, so anaphase fails and the cell is arrested in mitosis.
steps: Spindle fibres shorten to pull sister chromatids to opposite poles.
If they cannot shorten, the chromatids are not separated.
Anaphase cannot be completed.
The cell is stopped in mitosis, so it cannot divide.

questions.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of paclitaxel, using the cell cycle table and the tumour growth graph.
questions.answer: Paclitaxel appears effective: it increases the time cells spend in mitosis and cuts tumour growth to 0.42 g (about 66% less than placebo, about 53% less than drug X), but the evidence has limits.
steps: Table: as paclitaxel concentration rises from 0 to 10 000 nmol dm^-3, duration of mitosis rises from 1 h to 24 h and the mitotic index from 2% to 59%, so cells are held in mitosis and divide less; this fits it preventing spindle fibres shortening.
The effect is dose-dependent but levels off at high doses (21 to 24 h and 48% to 59% when concentration is raised ten-fold from 1000 to 10 000), so very high doses add little.
Graph: mean tumour mass increase is about 1.2 g with placebo, 0.9 g with drug X and 0.4 g with paclitaxel, about 66% less than placebo and 53% less than drug X.

The error bar for paclitaxel does not overlap those of placebo or drug X (top about 0.5 g against bottom about 0.7 g), so the difference is probably significant; drug X and placebo bars slightly overlap, so drug X may not be effective.

Limitations: the table is for human lung tumour cells but the graph is for mouse breast tumours; only one dose was tested in mice, for 21 days; sample size is not given; tumours still grew (not shrunk); mitotic index does not show cell death; side effects on healthy dividing cells (e.g. bone marrow, hair follicles) are not shown.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term phenotype.
questions.answer: The observable characteristics of an organism, produced by its genotype and environment.
steps: Phenotype is what can be observed or measured.
It is determined by genotype.
Environment can also influence it.
Examples include height, colour and blood group.

questions.question: Complete the table by writing a suitable heading for the right-hand column.
questions.answer: Genotype
steps: The right-hand column shows pairs of alleles (CC, c^ch c^ch, c^h c^h, cc) for each rabbit, which is its genotype.
The middle column is the phenotype (coat colour), so the heading for the right-hand column is genotype.

questions.question: Which row of the table gives the correct number of genes and alleles for coat colour in rabbits?
questions.answer: B: 1 gene, 4 alleles
steps: Coat colour is controlled by one gene (one locus), which has multiple alleles.
The table shows four different alleles of this gene: C, c^ch, c^h and c.
So there is 1 gene and 4 alleles: row B.

questions.question: Which row of the table names the types of graph to show sex and height variation in elephants?
questions.answer: B: sex = bar chart, height = histogram
steps: Sex is a discrete, categoric variable (male or female), so a bar chart with gaps between the bars is used.
Height is a continuous variable, so frequencies in height classes are plotted as a histogram with touching bars.
So the row is bar chart for sex and histogram for height: B.

questions.question: Male African elephants range in height from 3.2 m to 4.0 m; female African elephants range in height from 2.2 m to 2.6 m. Calculate how many times bigger the male African elephant is than the female African elephant.
questions.answer: 1.5 times (using mid-range heights)
steps: Male mid-range height = (3.2 + 4.0) / 2 = 3.6 m.
Female mid-range height = (2.2 + 2.6) / 2 = 2.4 m.
So the male is about 1.5 times the female's height.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term allele.
questions.answer: An alternative form of a gene, found at the same locus on a chromosome.
steps: A gene is a section of DNA at a locus.
Different versions of a gene are called alleles.
Alleles are found at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.
They can be dominant or recessive.

questions.question: Which genotype is Rhesus negative for all three genes (A ccddee, B ccddEe, C CcDdEe, D CCDDEE)?
questions.answer: A - ccddee
steps: Rhesus negative means no dominant C, D or E allele is present.
Each gene needs two recessive alleles to be negative.
ccddee has only recessive alleles for all three genes.
Option A is correct.

questions.question: Describe how a Rhesus antigen (glycoprotein) is produced from its polypeptide and transported to the cell surface membrane.
questions.answer: The polypeptide is made on ribosomes on the rough ER, glycosylated there, transported in vesicles to the Golgi for modification and packaging, then carried to the membrane in vesicles that fuse with it.
steps: The gene is transcribed to mRNA in the nucleus.
The polypeptide is translated on ribosomes attached to the rough ER.
The polypeptide enters the rough ER, where carbohydrate is added to form the glycoprotein.
Vesicles carry it to the Golgi apparatus, which modifies and packages it.
A vesicle carries the antigen to the membrane and fuses with it, releasing it onto the surface.

questions.question: Explain the variation in the colour of wheat seeds from a cross between two heterozygous plants.
questions.answer: Three genes each contribute a recessive allele additively, so the number of recessive alleles inherited varies and produces a range of seed colours.
steps: Three genes (A, B, C) affect seed colour, each with dominant and recessive alleles.
Each dominant allele adds to the colour; each recessive allele reduces it.
Random gamete combination gives different numbers of recessive alleles in offspring.
So many phenotypes with a range of seed colours appear.

questions.question: Explain why there is a large variation in the skin colour of offspring from this cross, using the diagram and your own knowledge.
questions.answer: Three polygenic genes each with two alleles give many allele combinations through independent assortment and random fertilisation, with additive effects and environmental influence producing continuous variation.
steps: Each parent is heterozygous for three genes, AaBbCc.
Independent assortment produces 8 different gamete types per parent.
Random fertilisation combines these gametes in many ways.
Each dominant allele adds to skin darkness, so the number of dominant alleles varies.
The additive effects give a range of shades (continuous variation).
Environmental factors such as sunlight can also change skin colour.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why an individual with the genotype AaBbCc may have a darker or lighter skin colour than predicted.
questions.answer: Environmental factors (e.g. more exposure to sunlight/UV, which stimulates melanin production) and epigenetic modification (e.g. less DNA methylation, so more expression of the melanin genes).
steps: Genotype is only one influence on phenotype, so identical genotypes (AaBbCc) can give different skin colours.
Environmental reason: more exposure to UV light or sunlight causes melanocytes to make more melanin, giving darker skin.

Epigenetic reason: changes such as DNA demethylation or histone acetylation near the genes for melanin production increase their transcription, so more pigment is made without any change to the DNA sequence.
Other acceptable ideas: other genes also affect skin colour, or hormone levels differ.

questions.question: Which description best fits a morula (A hollow pluripotent, B hollow totipotent, C solid pluripotent, D solid totipotent)?
questions.answer: D - a solid ball of totipotent cells
steps: A morula is an early embryo of about 16 cells.
It is a solid ball, not hollow, so options A and B are wrong.
Its cells are still totipotent, able to form all cell types.
Option D is correct.

questions.question: Suggest one function of the yolk in a fertilised fish egg cell.
questions.answer: It provides nutrients (food) for the developing embryo.
steps: Fish eggs develop outside the mother's body.
Developing embryos need energy and building materials.
The yolk is a store of nutrients (lipids and proteins).
So the yolk feeds the developing embryo.

questions.question: Explain how skeletal muscle cells can contain the same genes as morula cells but differ in structure and function.
questions.answer: Differential gene expression: only some genes are switched on in each cell type, controlled by transcription factors and epigenetic changes, so different proteins are made.
steps: All body cells contain the same DNA, from the zygote.
Cell differentiation switches on only the genes needed for each cell type.
In muscle cells, genes for actin and myosin are expressed.
Epigenetic changes such as methylation and histone modification switch other genes off.
So muscle cells produce specialised proteins and have a different structure and function.

questions.question: Calculate how many OVCAR8 cells out of 2000 were in interphase.
questions.answer: 1900 cells
steps: Read the mitotic index for OVCAR8 from the bar chart: 5%.
Number in mitosis = 5/100 x 2000 = 100 cells.
Cells not in mitosis are in interphase: 2000 - 100 = 1900 cells (95%).

questions.question: Which cancer cell culture has the highest proportion of cells undergoing nuclear division (A HOC8, B OVCAR5, C OVCAR8, D SKOV3)?
questions.answer: A: HOC8
steps: Mitotic index is the proportion of cells undergoing mitosis (nuclear division).
From the graph: OVCAR5 about 8.4%, OVCAR8 5%, HOC8 about 15% and SKOV3 about 9%.
HOC8 has the tallest bar, so it has the highest proportion of cells dividing.

questions.question: Explain why some people think cancer treatment research should not use embryonic stem cells.
questions.answer: Obtaining embryonic stem cells destroys a human embryo, which some people believe has the moral status of a person.
steps: Embryonic stem cells are taken from human embryos.
Obtaining them destroys the embryo.
Some people believe a human embryo has the right to life.
So they object to using such cells in research.

questions.question: Calculate the magnification of the pollen grain photograph to two significant figures.
questions.answer: x1500 (about 1465 before rounding)
steps: Magnification = length of scale bar in the image / actual length it represents.
The 20 um scale bar measures about 29 mm on the printed A4 page (about 104 px at 745 px per 210 mm); a ruler measurement of 29 mm to 30 mm is expected.
Convert: 29.3 mm = 29 300 um, so magnification = 29 300 / 20 = about 1465, which is x1500 to 2 significant figures.

questions.question: Describe how the generative nucleus results in the production of an embryo and endosperm tissue in a seed.
questions.answer: The generative nucleus divides to form two sperm nuclei; one fuses with the egg to form the embryo and the other fuses with two polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm.
steps: The pollen tube carries the generative nucleus to the ovule.
The generative nucleus divides by mitosis to form two male nuclei.
One male nucleus fuses with the egg cell, forming a diploid zygote that develops into the embryo.
The other fuses with two polar nuclei, forming a triploid nucleus that develops into endosperm.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term linkage for the flower colour and pollen grain size genes.
questions.answer: The genes are located close together on the same chromosome, so they tend to be inherited together.
steps: Linkage means two genes are on the same chromosome.
Because they are close, crossing over rarely separates them.
So the alleles are inherited together.
This is linkage.

questions.question: Which statistical test compares observed and expected phenotype frequencies (A chi squared, B correlation coefficient, C standard deviation, D Student's t-test)?
questions.answer: A - chi squared
steps: The test compares observed counts with expected counts.
Chi squared is used for frequency data like phenotype counts.
Correlation and t-tests are for other data types.
Option A is correct.

questions.question: Which term is used for different versions of a gene (A allele, B locus, C phenotype, D polygenic)?
questions.answer: A - allele
steps: Different versions of a gene are alleles.
A locus is the position of a gene, not a version.
Phenotype is an observable characteristic; polygenic describes inheritance.
Option A is correct.

questions.question: Explain how the phenotypes of an individual can show genetic linkage in the inheritance of two genes.
questions.answer: Linked genes on the same chromosome are inherited together, so certain phenotype combinations appear more often than expected from independent assortment.
steps: Two linked genes on chromosome 15 tend to be inherited together.
Their alleles stay together unless crossing over separates them.
So certain combinations of phenotypes appear more often than expected.
Recombinants are rarer, showing the genes are linked.

questions.question: Explain how different proteins can be synthesised from the mRNA after introns are removed.
questions.answer: Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons, giving different mRNAs and so different polypeptides.
steps: Introns are removed from pre-mRNA by splicing.
Exons can be joined in different combinations.
Each combination produces a different mature mRNA.
Each mRNA is translated into a different polypeptide.

questions.question: Calculate the volume of an unfertilised pike egg cell of diameter 2.3 mm, to one decimal place.
steps: Radius = 2.3 / 2 = 1.15 mm.
To one decimal place: 6.4 mm3.

questions.question: Explain why an egg cell has a larger volume than a sperm cell.
questions.answer: The egg stores yolk and nutrients to feed the developing embryo, whereas the sperm is streamlined to swim and carries only its genetic material.
steps: An egg cell stores yolk and organelles to nourish the early embryo.
A sperm cell contains little cytoplasm so it is small and streamlined.
Sperm only need to carry the paternal DNA to the egg.
So the egg is much larger.

questions.question: Which stage of mitosis is shown in the blastocyst cell photograph (A cytokinesis, B metaphase, C prophase, D telophase)?
questions.answer: B: metaphase
steps: The photograph shows a spindle with the chromosomes lined up in a compact band across the middle of the cell (the equator).

In prophase the chromosomes are condensing and not yet aligned, and the nuclear envelope breaks down; in telophase two separate groups of chromosomes lie at opposite poles; in cytokinesis the cell membrane pinches in.
Chromosomes aligned at the equator on spindle fibres means metaphase.

questions.question: State how the blastocyst cell was treated to show the stage of mitosis.
questions.answer: It was stained with a dye (e.g. acetic orcein or a DNA stain) that binds to the chromosomes.
steps: Chromosomes are too faint to see in an unstained cell.
A stain that binds DNA is applied to the cell.
The stained chromosomes become visible under the microscope.
So the stage of mitosis can be identified.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of a morula with that of a blastocyst.
questions.answer: Both are balls of cells formed by mitosis; the morula is solid, whereas the blastocyst is hollow with a fluid-filled cavity, an outer trophoblast and an inner cell mass.
steps: Both are early embryos made by mitotic division of the zygote.
The morula is a solid ball of cells.
The blastocyst is hollow, with a fluid-filled blastocoel.
The blastocyst has an outer trophoblast layer and an inner cell mass.

questions.question: Describe the adaptations of a sperm cell that allow it to move.
questions.answer: A flagellum for propulsion and many mitochondria in the midpiece to supply ATP for movement.
steps: The flagellum (tail) is a whip-like structure that propels the cell.
Its microtubules slide to produce a wave-like beat.
Many mitochondria in the midpiece produce ATP by aerobic respiration.
The streamlined head reduces drag in water.

questions.question: Give two conclusions for the investigation of sperm speed in February and March.
questions.answer: Sperm speed decreased with time after release into water in both months; sperm were faster in March than in February at every time.
steps: Conclusion 1: mean speed falls as time after release increases in both months, e.g. in February from about 195 um s^-1 at 10 s to about 55 um s^-1 at 40 s (March about 230 to 80).
Conclusion 2: at each time (10, 20, 30 and 40 s) the March sperm swim faster than the February sperm, e.g. about 230 against 195 um s^-1 at 10 s.
The sperm probably slow down as their energy (ATP) is used up or the cells age after release.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a blastocyst.
questions.answer: A hollow ball of cells with a fluid-filled cavity (blastocoel), an outer trophoblast layer and an inner cell mass at one end.
steps: A blastocyst is a hollow ball of cells.
The cavity inside is filled with fluid (blastocoel).
The outer layer is the trophoblast.
A cluster of inner cells forms the inner cell mass.

questions.topic: Cells In Mitosis From Mitotic Index
questions.question: Calculate the number of cells in structure A that were in mitosis, given 60 cells and a mitotic index of 15%.
questions.answer: 9 cells
steps: Mitotic index = number in mitosis / total cells x 100.
Number in mitosis = 15% of 60.
So 9 cells are in mitosis.

questions.question: Explain how histone modification and DNA methylation alter the activation of genes as cells become pluripotent.
questions.answer: Histone acetylation loosens chromatin so genes are transcribed; DNA methylation and methylated histones condense chromatin or block transcription factors, switching genes off.
steps: Histones are proteins around which DNA is wound.
Acetylation of histones loosens chromatin, allowing transcription and switching genes on.
Methylation of DNA (at cytosine) prevents transcription factors from binding.
Methylated histones or DNA condense chromatin, switching genes off.
These changes restrict which genes are active, so cells become more specialised.

questions.question: Which statement about the pluripotent stem cells in bone marrow is correct (A all cell types, B all except extraembryonic, C some types, D red blood cells only)?
questions.answer: B - they can produce all types of cell except extraembryonic cells
steps: Pluripotent cells can form most cell types of the body.
They cannot form extraembryonic tissues such as the placenta.
They are not limited to only some types, so C is wrong.
Option B is correct.

questions.question: Describe the role of the rough endoplasmic reticulum in the synthesis of haemoglobin.
questions.answer: Ribosomes on the rough ER make the globin polypeptide chains, which are folded and then transported in vesicles to the Golgi.
steps: Ribosomes on the rough ER translate mRNA into globin polypeptides.
The rough ER folds the polypeptides into their correct shape.
Transport vesicles carry the polypeptides to the Golgi apparatus.
The haem group is added after the polypeptide is made, not by the RER.

questions.question: Describe the changes in the percentages of polypeptides in red blood cells before and after birth, using the graph.
questions.answer: Alpha stays constant at about 50%; gamma stays high (about 47%) then falls to almost 0% by 6 months after birth; beta rises slowly then rapidly around birth to about 48% by 6 months after birth.
steps: Alpha: rises from about 8% at 8 months before birth to about 50% by about 6.5 months before birth and then stays constant at about 50% for the rest of the period.

Gamma: rises to about 47% by 6 months before birth and stays at that level until about 3 months before birth, then falls to about 40% at birth, about 18% at 2 months after birth, and almost 0% by 6 months after birth.

Beta: starts at about 1.5% at 7 months before birth, rising slowly to about 4% by 3 months before birth and about 12% at birth, then rising rapidly to about 35% at 2 months after birth and about 48% at 6 months after birth.
Gamma and beta curves cross at about 25% roughly 1.5 months after birth: fetal haemoglobin (alpha + gamma) is replaced by adult haemoglobin (alpha + beta).

questions.question: Explain how epigenetic modification could result in these changes in haemoglobin polypeptides.
questions.answer: Epigenetic changes such as DNA methylation and histone modification switch the fetal globin gene off and the adult globin gene on at different times, altering which polypeptides are made.
steps: Fetal and adult haemoglobin use different globin genes.
Epigenetic modification (methylation or histone changes) controls which globin gene is active.
After birth, the fetal gene is switched off and the adult gene is switched on.
This changes the proportions of polypeptides made, without any change in the DNA sequence.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term locus.
questions.answer: The position of a gene on a chromosome.
steps: A locus is a fixed position on a chromosome.
Alleles of a gene are found at the same locus.
It is where a gene is located.
So the locus is the gene's position.

questions.question: Explain how these alleles can produce fruit flies with different coloured eyes.
questions.answer: Different alleles have different base sequences, so they code for proteins with different functions, producing different amounts of pigment and so different eye colours.
steps: Each allele has a different base sequence from mutation.
Different base sequences give different amino acid sequences.
So the protein (e.g. an enzyme in pigment production) can differ in function.
Different pigment amounts or types produce different eye colours.

questions.question: Explain how one gene can give rise to either a female or a male fly, given the Dsx-F and Dsx-M proteins.
questions.answer: Alternative splicing of the same pre-mRNA produces different mRNAs in males and females, giving the female-specific or male-specific Dsx protein.
steps: Both Dsx-F and Dsx-M come from one gene.
The pre-mRNA is spliced differently in each sex.
Different exons are included or removed.
This gives different mRNAs, which are translated into the female or male protein.
The sex-specific protein then directs female or male development.

questions.question: Explain how histone modification can affect gene expression.
questions.answer: Histone acetylation loosens chromatin so transcription factors can reach the gene and switch it on; methylation can tighten chromatin and switch it off.
steps: Histones are proteins around which DNA is wound into nucleosomes.
Acetylation adds acetyl groups, neutralising the positive charge on histones.
This weakens the attraction to DNA, so chromatin loosens.
Transcription factors can then access the gene, so it is expressed.
Methylation of histones can instead tighten chromatin and switch the gene off.

questions.question: Draw a mammalian sperm cell showing the acrosome, nucleus and a mitochondrion, and label them.
questions.answer: A sperm drawing with an oval head containing the nucleus, an acrosome cap over the front of the head, a midpiece with mitochondria, and a long flagellum.
steps: Draw an oval head; label the acrosome as a cap over the front of the head.
Draw the nucleus filling most of the head behind the acrosome.
Draw a midpiece behind the head with a mitochondrion inside, labelled.
Draw a long flagellum (tail) extending from the midpiece.

questions.question: Calculate the volume of a human egg cell of radius 50 (micrometres) using the sphere formula.
steps: Volume = 4/3 x pi x r^3.
In standard form: 5.2 x 10^5 um3. The unit is micrometres, consistent with the surface area given.

questions.question: Give the surface area to volume ratio of the egg cell, given surface area 31 416 um2.
steps: Surface area = 31 416 um2 and volume = 523 599 um3.
Written as x : 1: 0.06 : 1.
A small ratio means the surface area is small relative to volume, which limits exchange, so specialised eggs must rely on other adaptations.

questions.question: Explain three ways in which a mammalian egg cell is specialised for its functions.
questions.answer: It is large with a food store for early development; it has a zona pellucida and cortical granules that prevent polyspermy; and it has a haploid nucleus to combine with the sperm.
steps: Large size and cytoplasm store nutrients for early development.
The zona pellucida and cortical granules block multiple sperm entering.
It contains a haploid nucleus so that fertilisation restores the diploid number.
It has many mitochondria and ribosomes to support early development.

questions.question: A fertilised egg cell develops into a morula and then a blastocyst. Which of the following are correct statements? 1 A blastocyst contains pluripotent stem cells; 2 A blastocyst is a hollow ball of cells whereas a morula is not; 3 Both of these structures contain cells which divide by meiosis. Options: A 1 and 2 only; B 1 and 3 only; C 2 and 3 only; D 1, 2 and 3.
questions.answer: A - 1 and 2 only
steps: Statement 1 is correct: the blastocyst has pluripotent stem cells.
Statement 2 is correct: the blastocyst is hollow and the morula is solid.
Statement 3 is wrong: embryo cells divide by mitosis, not meiosis.
So option A is correct.

questions.question: Describe what happens to DNA during interphase.
questions.answer: DNA is replicated during the S phase of interphase, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids.
steps: Interphase includes the S phase.
During S phase, DNA is replicated semi-conservatively.
Each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids.
The DNA is uncoiled as chromatin for transcription and replication.

questions.question: Name the stage of mitosis that follows prophase.
questions.answer: Metaphase
steps: Mitosis has four stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.
In prophase, chromosomes condense and the spindle forms.
Next, chromosomes line up at the equator.
This stage is metaphase.

questions.question: Explain how an error in meiosis could give a zygote with three copies of chromosome 13.
questions.answer: Non-disjunction: homologous chromosomes (or sister chromatids) fail to separate, so a gamete gets two copies; fertilisation with a normal gamete gives three copies.
steps: In meiosis I or II, chromosome 13 fails to separate properly (non-disjunction).
One gamete receives both copies of chromosome 13 instead of one.
Fertilisation with a normal gamete (one copy) gives a zygote with three copies.
This trisomy causes Patau syndrome.

questions.question: Which row of the table is correct for the morula and blastocyst formed from the zygote?
questions.answer: C: zygote is totipotent; cells in the blastocyst inner mass are pluripotent
steps: A zygote can form every cell type, including the extra-embryonic tissues such as the trophoblast, so it is totipotent.
Inner cell mass cells of the blastocyst can form most body cell types but not extra-embryonic tissue, so they are pluripotent.
This matches row C (totipotent, then pluripotent).

questions.question: Suggest a reason why part of chromosome 13 can attach to a different chromosome during prophase I when a gamete is formed.
questions.answer: The two chromosomes share similar (homologous) sequences, so they can pair and exchange parts during meiosis.
steps: In prophase I, chromosomes pair with similar sequences.
Part of chromosome 13 may share sequences with another chromosome.
Mispairing between these similar sequences allows an exchange of segments.
This is called translocation.

questions.question: Explain how DNA methylation can alter the expression of some genes.
questions.answer: Methylation of cytosine bases silences a gene by blocking transcription factor binding and promoting condensed chromatin.
steps: Methyl groups are added to cytosine bases, usually in CpG sequences.
Methylated DNA blocks transcription factors from binding to the promoter.
Methylation also attracts proteins that condense chromatin.
So the gene is switched off.

questions.question: Explain why epigenetic changes such as DNA methylation are passed on by mitosis.
questions.answer: During DNA replication, the methylation pattern on the parent strand is copied onto the new strand, so daughter cells inherit it.
steps: Each DNA molecule is replicated semi-conservatively in S phase.
Enzymes copy the methylation pattern from the old strand onto the new strand.
Each daughter cell therefore inherits the same methylation pattern.
So the epigenetic state is passed on through mitosis.

questions.question: Suggest how cell damage could lead to activation of the sox2 gene.
questions.answer: Damage releases signalling molecules that bind receptors and activate transcription factors, which switch on the sox2 gene.
steps: Damaged cells release chemical signals.
The signals bind receptors on nearby cells.
This activates transcription factors that bind the sox2 gene promoter.
Transcription of sox2 is switched on.

questions.question: Give one difference between a pluripotent stem cell and a totipotent stem cell.
questions.answer: A totipotent cell can form all cell types including extraembryonic tissues and a whole organism; a pluripotent cell cannot form extraembryonic tissues.
steps: Totipotent cells can form every cell type and a whole organism.
Pluripotent cells can form most cell types.
Pluripotent cells cannot form extraembryonic tissues such as the placenta.
So totipotency is wider than pluripotency.

questions.question: Explain how three different active mRNA strands are produced from one strand of pre-mRNA.
questions.answer: Alternative splicing removes introns and joins different combinations of exons, producing three different mRNA strands.
steps: Pre-mRNA contains introns and exons.
Introns are removed by splicing.
The exons are joined in different combinations.
Each combination gives a different active mRNA, which codes for a different protein.

questions.topic: Approval Of Starfish Stem Cell Research
questions.question: Suggest why society has approved the use of stem cells taken from starfish for research.
questions.answer: Starfish stem cells come from animals, not humans, so they raise fewer ethical concerns, and they can help research into regeneration and medicine.
steps: Starfish are not human, so the cells raise fewer ethical objections.
The stem cells are pluripotent, so they can form many cell types.
They can be used to study how cells specialise.
This can help research into regeneration and medical treatments.
